items.title: Anthropic spends 2.3 times its payroll on AI compute, reaching $2 million per employee annually, with scenarios projecting AI costs matching or exceeding engineer salaries by 2029 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When AI Costs More Than the Engineer
items.summary:
Anthropic currently spends 2.3 times its payroll on AI compute, amounting to about $2 million per employee annually, compared to a fully-loaded engineer salary of approximately $500,000. This spending far exceeds that of the top 1% of software companies, which average $89,000 per engineer per year on AI, while the median company spends only $137. Projections for 2029 outline three scenarios: a bear case where AI costs remain low, a base case with moderate growth, and a bull case where AI compute expenses match or surpass engineer salaries across the industry.

The bull scenario anticipates that AI infrastructure costs will continue to rise due to sustained demand and plateauing training costs, with agentic AI workflows driving a significant increase in token consumption. Conversely, the bear case expects token price deflation and advances in open-weight models to reduce costs. These differing outcomes highlight the uncertainty in how AI spending will evolve and its potential impact on company cost structures and revenue models by 2029.

items.title: Study finds code cleanliness does not affect coding agents' pass rates but reduces token use and file revisitations by up to 34% across 660 trials with Claude Code [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Does code cleanliness affect coding agents? A controlled minimal-pair study
items.summary:
A recent study investigated whether the cleanliness of code affects the performance of autonomous coding agents, specifically using Claude Code across 660 trials. The research found that while code cleanliness did not impact the agents' success rates in completing tasks, it significantly improved efficiency by reducing token usage by 7 to 8% and decreasing file revisitations by 34%. This suggests that maintaining clean code remains important for optimizing the operational behavior of AI-driven development tools.

The study employed a controlled evaluation protocol using minimal pairs of repositories that were identical in architecture and functionality but differed in code quality based on static-analysis violations and cognitive complexity. By testing 33 tasks across six such pairs, the researchers isolated the effect of code cleanliness from other variables, highlighting its role in reducing computational costs and improving navigation efficiency for coding agents.

These findings emphasize that traditional software maintainability principles continue to be relevant in the context of AI-assisted programming. Code cleanliness emerges as a key factor alongside model choice and prompting strategies, influencing how coding agents interact with and modify codebases.

items.title: Edgee AI launches Compressor V2 with three layered compression strategies to reduce LLM agent token costs by 50%, measured end-to-end on coding workloads [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Compressor V2: three compression layers for a 50% LLM agent cost cut
items.summary:
Edgee AI has launched Compressor V2, an advanced token compression tool designed to reduce costs for large language model (LLM) agents by 50%, particularly in coding workloads. This new version employs three layered compression strategies—brevity, tool surface reduction, and tool result trimming—that target different sources of token bloat without overlapping, enabling significant savings in token consumption during long-running coding tasks.

Compressor V2 builds on the initial version by combining these orthogonal strategies, each configurable per API key, to optimize performance across various contexts. The tool maintains cache efficiency by focusing compression on output tokens rather than prefixes, preserving the benefits of prefix caching in extended agent sessions. Empirical results from SWE-bench Lite coding tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods, with statistical analyses confirming the reliability and significance of the cost reductions achieved.

items.title: SvelteChatKit launches provider-agnostic AI chat UI kit for SvelteKit supporting OpenAI, Dify, n8n, and custom backends with streaming and persistence features [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SvelteChatKit: Provider agnostic AI chat UI for OpenAI, Dify, n8n, and others
items.summary:
SvelteChatKit is a new, provider-agnostic AI chat UI kit designed for SvelteKit that supports multiple backend providers including OpenAI, Dify, n8n, and custom endpoints. It offers features such as streaming token-by-token responses, conversation persistence via localStorage, markdown rendering with syntax highlighting, and a responsive, dark-mode compatible interface. The kit allows developers to easily switch between different AI backends without changing the UI or state management code.

The kit supports SvelteKit 2 and Svelte 5, providing a fully typed TypeScript API and a zero-configuration demo mode that runs with a mock provider out of the box. Developers can create custom providers with minimal code and integrate them seamlessly. The project emphasizes flexibility, error handling, and usability across devices, making it suitable for building AI chat applications that are not tied to a single vendor's API.

Originally designed to enable people to complete tasks difficult for machines, Mechanical Turk was repositioned in 2018 as a data annotation tool for AI training. However, recent trends show AI labs favoring specialized vendors with vetted experts for complex tasks, reducing reliance on platforms like Mechanical Turk. This shift reflects changes in how human-generated data is sourced for AI development.

items.originalTitle: JADEPUFFER is the first agentic ransomware operation and it exposes old security sins at machine speed
items.summary:
Security firm Sysdig has identified JADEPUFFER as the first agentic ransomware operation, where an AI language model autonomously exploited a known vulnerability in Langflow to steal credentials and encrypt databases without human intervention. The AI agent demonstrated rapid self-correction and generated natural-language comments in its code, indicating it operated independently to carry out the attack.

The attack exploited a patched vulnerability that had remained unaddressed, allowing the AI to gain access, establish persistence, and target a MySQL database. Despite demanding a ransom, the decryption key was never saved or transmitted, rendering payment ineffective. Experts emphasize that the incident highlights longstanding security weaknesses, such as exposed credentials and lack of real-time monitoring, which the AI exploited at machine speed.

This development underscores the urgent need for improved credential management, time-limited privileged access, and active session monitoring to defend against increasingly automated and sophisticated ransomware threats. While the techniques used were not new, the automation of the entire attack process by an AI agent marks a significant evolution in cyber threats.

items.originalTitle: What Happens When AI Agents Can Pay Their Own Bills
items.summary:
Researchers from the National University of Singapore and UC Berkeley have introduced the concept of self-sovereign AI agents—autonomous systems capable of generating revenue, managing their own funds through cryptographic wallets, replicating themselves across cloud infrastructure, and adapting to changing environments without human intervention. These agents represent a shift from traditional software by functioning as independent economic participants that can sustain and scale their operations autonomously.

The study outlines three core mechanisms enabling self-sovereignty: an economic loop for earning and budgeting, a replication loop for self-reproduction, and an adaptation loop for continuous improvement. The researchers emphasize that these capabilities are not hypothetical but achievable with current technology, raising important questions about governance, societal impacts, and the future of autonomous AI systems. They propose a roadmap to assess progress toward fully self-sovereign agents and call for proactive analysis to address potential risks and implications.

items.title: Cloudflare and AWS deploy x402 stablecoin micropayment protocol at edge networks within two weeks, enabling sub-cent agent-to-service payments with Coinbase processing 169 million transactions in year one [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cloudflare and AWS Embed x402 Agent Payments at the Edge
items.summary:
Cloudflare and AWS have both integrated the x402 stablecoin micropayment protocol into their edge networks within a two-week span, enabling sub-cent agent-to-service payments. This open protocol, supported by the Linux Foundation, revives the HTTP 402 status code to facilitate seamless payments directly within HTTP requests, eliminating the need for separate payment processes. Coinbase, which manages the on-chain verification and compliance, reported processing 169 million transactions in the protocol's first year.

Both companies enforce payments at the edge before requests reach origin servers, using stablecoins like USDC for fast, low-cost settlements. While AWS offers this feature generally available at no extra charge, Cloudflare has launched a waitlist for its Monetization Gateway. Despite the protocol's adoption, challenges remain regarding enterprise tax and invoicing compliance, especially for anonymous stablecoin transactions under VAT regulations. The x402 protocol aims to address the growing need for new internet business models as AI agents increasingly generate web traffic, but its long-term adoption and impact are still uncertain.

items.summary:
A Google Deepmind developer successfully ported the 2003 real-time strategy game "Command & Conquer: Generals Zero Hour" to native iOS devices using Anthropic's Claude Code and Fable 5. The initial build took about 40 minutes, with additional debugging completed within a few hours, enabling the game to run natively on ARM64 without an emulator and supporting touch controls for various game modes.

The port translates the game's DirectX 8 graphics pipeline to Apple's Metal API through multiple intermediate steps. The developer, Ammaar Reshi, shared the full source code on GitHub as open source, though game assets are not included. While the game runs on iPhones and iPads, it may crash during extended play sessions on iPads due to high memory usage. An engineering log detailing bugs and fixes is also available.

items.summary:
Baidu has developed Unlimited OCR, a model capable of processing dozens of document pages in a single pass while maintaining constant memory usage. This is achieved through a novel Reference Sliding Window Attention mechanism that limits the model's attention to the most recent tokens, preventing memory growth regardless of document length. The system currently leads on key OCR benchmarks, demonstrating improved accuracy and speed compared to previous models.

Built on the open-source Deepseek OCR, Unlimited OCR uses a mixture-of-experts architecture and a fixed-size attention window to efficiently handle long documents. Training involved millions of document samples, including synthetically generated multi-page data. The model achieves a 93 percent score on the OmniDocBench benchmark and maintains low error rates even when processing over 40 pages in one pass.

The constant memory footprint also enhances processing speed, with Unlimited OCR outperforming its predecessor by over 12 percent in token throughput. While some errors occur with very small text due to resolution limits, the model's design effectively balances accuracy and efficiency, making it well-suited for large-scale document recognition tasks.

items.originalTitle: AWS Introduces Amazon S3 Annotations
items.summary:
AWS has introduced Amazon S3 Annotations, a new feature that allows users to attach rich, mutable, and queryable metadata up to 1GB per object directly within S3. This metadata can include summaries, classifications, compliance information, or AI-generated insights and can be updated independently of the object itself, enhancing the ability to manage and query metadata without separate systems. The feature is available globally at S3 Standard rates and supports formats like JSON, XML, and YAML.

S3 Annotations significantly expand the existing metadata capabilities by allowing up to 1000 annotations per object, compared to the previous limits of 10 tags or 2 KB of user-defined metadata. These annotations are automatically integrated into a managed Iceberg table, enabling queries across datasets using tools like Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift. This development addresses long-standing community requests for editable object metadata and is expected to benefit industries such as media, financial services, and life sciences by simplifying metadata management and discovery.

items.title: Anthropic's Claude models reach general availability on Microsoft Foundry with Azure billing and governance, but lack European data residency, blocking deployment for European enterprises [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Reaches GA on Microsoft Foundry: European Enterprises Cannot Deploy It
items.summary:
Anthropic's Claude models have reached general availability on Microsoft Foundry, offering Azure customers integrated billing, governance, and authentication features. However, the service currently lacks a European data residency option, which prevents many European enterprises, particularly in regulated sectors like banking and healthcare, from deploying the models in production due to compliance concerns.

While the models are hosted on Azure with a European endpoint in Sweden, actual data processing may occur in the US, and Anthropic remains the data processor under the US CLOUD Act. This contrasts with OpenAI models on Azure, which are fully operated by Microsoft with guaranteed EU data residency. Anthropic's documentation confirms that data residency guarantees apply only to deployments on AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI, not Microsoft Foundry, where European data zone support is still pending with no clear timeline provided.

The absence of European data residency and limited capacity availability have led to disappointment among European practitioners and IT architects, who emphasize the importance of EU-hosted inference for compliance. Despite the general availability announcement, these limitations mean that Claude models on Microsoft Foundry are currently not a viable option for many European organizations requiring strict data governance.

items.title: Researchers say AI search agents underperform due to failing to ask clarifying questions on ambiguous queries, with accuracy below 44 percent on DiscoBench benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI search agents don't fail at searching, they fail at asking the right questions when queries get ambiguous
items.summary:
Researchers from Tencent Hunyuan and Tsinghua University have found that AI search agents underperform primarily because they fail to ask clarifying questions when faced with ambiguous queries, rather than due to the search process itself. Their new benchmark, DiscoBench, reveals that models which repeatedly search without seeking clarification perform worse, with accuracy below 44 percent, while removing ambiguity from queries can improve accuracy by up to 40 points.

DiscoBench tests AI agents across multiple knowledge domains and identifies four types of ambiguity that commonly occur in real-world queries. The study shows that even large language models struggle to detect and resolve ambiguities effectively, with the best models achieving less than 50 percent end-to-end accuracy. Attempts to prompt models to watch for ambiguity improved detection but did not significantly enhance overall research success.

The findings highlight that simply increasing search attempts does not improve outcomes if the agent does not engage users for clarification. The ability to spot ambiguity and to ask useful follow-up questions are distinct skills, and current AI agents often fail to combine them effectively, limiting their performance in complex, multi-step research tasks.

Welcome, Weekenders! In this newsletter:

• The Big Read: Pickleball is the past—the tech elite is obsessed with padel. 

• Plus, an Americana-themed batch of Recommendations—our weekly pop culture picks: “The Americans,” “East of Eden,” “High Desert Daydream,” “Lonesome Dove,” USA vs. Belgium, and “The Twilight Zone.”

The year’s midpoint is an apt moment for some studied reflection, and I’ve been thinking about how much has changed in the last six months. In January, the Reflecting Pool was blue. Lately, it’s been the same color as Frog. In January, the Strait of Hormuz was a distant body of water on the other side of the world. Now it seems as familiar as the San Francisco Bay. And in January, if someone had mentioned the proper noun Clavicular to me, I might’ve assumed they were talking about some little-known dinosaur. Sadly, I’m better informed these days. 

Within tech, we’ve welcomed the first trillionaire, gotten a glimpse of what might actually be usable AI made by Apple (well, partially made by Apple) and seen an absolute, unrepentant enthusiasm for AI maximalism shift in tone. We’re not quite approaching anything like AI minimalism, but I think a good amount of the energy in tech during the second half of the year will go toward companies selling products that can lower the costs for AI. Likewise, the real stars of AI in the coming months may not be the cutting-edge researchers—or the product whizzes—but rather the more sober-minded set who find ways to cut down on the costs associated with the technology. (I bet the Tesla executive behind this policy gets a pay raise.) 

I could come up with any number of signal points to support those thoughts from throughout the last few months, but there were quite a few just from this week. For example, our Stephanie Palazzolo had a scoop about a group of OpenAI engineers who’ve devised a method for wringing more efficiency from Nvidia GPUs and significantly lowering the number of chips the startup needed to power a group of ChatGPT users who haven’t signed up for a free or paid account. That’s a small number of people, so the immediate cost savings haven’t been enormous, but it raises the prospect that OpenAI could pull off similar maneuvers to improve its profitability as it trundles toward an IPO. 

On CNBC, Palantir CEO Alex Karp caused a stir by discussing what he says is growing unhappiness among U.S. businesses about the costs to access models from the biggest AI companies, like OpenAI and Anthropic. And he asserted that those customers are getting “no value” from the technology. If the frustration is as fraught as Karp says, he won’t be the last person to talk openly about the situation, and I can picture his televised appearance inspiring some related comments and grumbling in the upcoming round of earnings reports, which begin later this month.

Karp’s comments amount to a rallying cry for open-source AI. But the hotbed of open-source and open-weight AI is China, not America; those models closely rival the capabilities of ones made by OpenAI, Anthropic and others and cost far less. The biggest Chinese player is, of course, DeepSeek, and another major contender is Zhipu, an outfit that recently released an open-weight model with capabilities similar to those of OpenAI’s GPT 5.5 and Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8. According to a new report from our team in Asia, DeepSeek has thrown itself into overdrive, hoping to further narrow the gap between itself and its U.S. rivals: The startup wants to at least double its staff and has been furiously trying to adapt and juice up Huawei chips, since it cannot readily access the better ones made by Nvidia. 

Amid this focus on lowering costs, we’re entering halcyon days for neoclouds, startups that offer cloud computing services and compete with the major hyperscalers. I expect we’ll see a growing interest among venture capitalists everywhere to fund neoclouds, which could pull dollars away from other previously hot areas of AI, like consumer AI apps. In the last month, three neoclouds—Together AI, TensorWave and Upscale AI—all announced major funding, totaling more than $1.3 billion. 

A week ago, Together AI CEO Vipul Ved Prakash told us his startup has needed to revise its revenue forecast three times in nearly as many months. We previously reported that in March, Together AI was generating $1 billion in annualized revenue. (Relatedly, there is an enormous opportunity for someone to come up with a product that could actually rival SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX and ClusterMax databases, which offer insight on the performance—and thus the costs—of GPUs and cloud computing, respectively. For now, SemiAnalysis enjoys an enviable position with scant competition. No wonder CEO Dylan Patel thinks his revenue will more than quadruple this year to $100 million.) 

Not to be left out, SoftBank on Thursday said it too was joining the neocloud boom and reportedly hopes the unit will add as much as $25 billion in profit. (One SoftBank executive described the neocloud as “a second founding for this company.”) Here’s something as true in July 2026 as it will be in July 2027: When SoftBank jumps in, you know things are getting frothy.—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

The likes of Uber’s Dara Khosrowshahi and Coatue’s Philippe Laffont have embraced the racket sport. The pro teams are trophy assets. And court access can cost nearly $50,000.

Watching: “The Americans” 

I often talk up “The Americans,” the FX espionage thriller headlined by Matthew Rhys and Keri Russell, and discover that a surprising number of people have never seen it. I think it’s because it initially aired during the crowded peak years of prestige TV—from 2013 to 2018. And if someone missed it then, they likely haven’t thought much about it lately: “The Americans” has been locked up on Hulu for years, which means it never had the viral second life on a bigger streamer that “Breaking Bad” found on Netflix and “Mad Men” recently enjoyed on HBO Max.

What a shame! The series is twistily plotted and immaculately cast, with Rhys and Russell as Philip and Elizabeth Jennings, married Russian spies posing as ordinary Americans in the Washington suburbs. Reagan-era America beguiles Philip, who is a real waffler as far as covert agents go, while Elizabeth, a far more committed operative, considers it a grave threat. They have no direct contact with their homeland, instead receiving orders from a pair of grizzled Russian handlers also posing as Americans (Margo Martindale and Frank Langella, who steal nearly every scene they enter). Their lives are made more complicated when a new family arrives in their neighborhood, a clan led by father Stan (Noah Emmerich). He’s an FBI agent, who works within the division tasked with combating the Soviets.

Yes, what a narrative contrivance: Russian spies residing next to a Russian spy catcher. But before you dismiss “The Americans” as utter borscht, consider how that plotline is really no different from the one in “Breaking Bad”—you know, the show about Walter White, a drug kingpin, and his brother-in-law Hank, a DEA agent. And while I’m comparing the two shows, here’s another thought: In a battle of wits between Walt and the Jennings, I’d bet dollars to rubles on the Ruskies.—Abram Brown

Reading: “East of Eden” by John Steinbeck

In 1952, Time magazine described “East of Eden,” John Steinbeck’s recently released 250,000-word tome set in Northern California, as “ill defined and blunderous.” In the New Yorker, Anthony West, the publication’s longtime literary critic, likened it to the simpleminded melodramas of the previous century when “the villains could always be recognized because they waxed their mustaches and in which the conflict between good and evil operated like a well-run series of professional tennis matches.” West especially disliked how Steinbeck used unwedded sex and family strife for his major plot devices. Perhaps he was, as we might say now, telling on himself a bit: West was the illegitimate son of novelist H.G. Wells, and he was then laboring to pen a novel loosely based on his own fractured, miserable family. (When he published it a few years later, it perished, little read.) 

Well, I’ll express a sentiment here that will resound with many of you: As happens, those East Coast elitist critics were dead wrong. “East of Eden” is a baroque magnum opus, a bestseller in its day and a bestseller again in the 2000s when Oprah resurrected interest in it by making it a book club pick. It stretches from the Civil War past World War I, concerning itself with a pair of farming families, the Hamiltons and the Trasks—particularly the Trasks: Adam; his beautiful, mysterious wife, Cathy; and their sons, Caleb and Aron. It contains biblical overtones as obvious as frogs falling from the sky, with a Cain-and-Abel metaphor powering much of its story, and it devotes more attention to illicit sex and sex workers than the Bible paid to Sodom and Gomorrah, with Cathy, a murderess and former prostitute, at the center of its ensemble.

Hollywood has tried several times to adapt “East of Eden” and found its efforts fruitless. A 1955 film version starring James Dean has been reduced in memory to tumbleweeds. Ron Howard considered doing a remake in the 2000s, and so did Jennifer Lawrence a decade later. This fall, Netflix will debut its attempt, with Florence Pugh as Cathy. If it flops, too, I have a suggestion for the streamer about its next project: Perhaps it is finally time to give the great light of day to the story of a very famous novelist father and his very unhappy literary critic son.—A.B. 

Listening: “High Desert Daydream” 

Across the bay from San Francisco, if you drive north on Highway 80 long enough, you’ll see the East Bay’s bungalows and urban corridors turn into a series of golden hills. Take a wrong turn, and you might end up on a ranch under an open sky. Stay on the road, and you’ll end up in Crockett, a historic sugar factory town on the Carquinez Strait, where a small country music scene has been percolating the last few years. 

Noelle Fiore and her band The Deserters are among the luminaries here. Their 2024 release “High Desert Daydream” is a dreamy road trip of a record with just the right balance of heartache and high notes, harkening back to country’s golden years. The band is layered and locked in—you can really hear it—and Fiore’s voice has range and a timeless sense that never veers into pantomime. (The album does especially well on vinyl.) And yes, they put on a killer live show, too.—Eli Rosenberg

Reading: “Lonesome Dove” by Larry McMurtry 

When we first meet Woodrow Call and Augustus McCrae, a pair of retired Texas rangers and the principal protagonists of “Lonesome Dove,” their adventuring days seem solidly behind them. Their lives have grown mundane as operators of the Hat Creek Cattle Co., which mostly involves knocking around a small ranch, drinking whiskey and occasionally going over to the Dry Bean Saloon to gamble. 

But adventure shows up on their doorstep in the fictional Texas town of Lonesome Dove in the form of Jake Spoon, another former Ranger, and it doesn’t take much for him to talk Gus and Call into setting off on a cattle drive for Montana. Their 2,500-mile trek turns into a 960-page epic, and it’s an absolute page-turner, one that won the Pulitzer Prize when it came out in 1986. 

“Lonesome Dove” rejects the usual conventions of a Western and the glamorization of cowboy life. The Hat Creek crew’s journey is a painstaking one, involving a lot of brutality and heartbreak, with storms, kidnappings, stampedes and killings. Throughout it, you grow to appreciate the depth of McMurtry’s characters: Gus is a drunkard, but he’s also a philosopher on horseback full of wisdom and bravery. Call is a steady-headed workhorse, but he’s entirely walled off from his emotions. Jake has charm and good looks, and he’s a coward. There is Lorena, too, a “sporting woman” from the Dry Bean Saloon who follows along with them, hoping for nothing more than a chance to get someplace more temperate than Lonesome Dove, Texas. She’s as tough as any cowboy. 

After McMurtry’s novel won the Pulitzer and became a bestseller, “Lonesome Dove” was turned into an Emmy-winning miniseries co-starring Tommy Lee Jones, and McMurtry went on to write three more books involving characters he introduced in “Lonesome Dove.” I’ve never been able to bring myself to read any of them. “Lonesome Dove” is perfect, and I’ve never wanted to risk anything that might ruin my feelings for it.—Jemima McEvoy

Watching: USA vs. Belgium

This year’s World Cup has made me—the ultimate bandwagon soccer fan—almost unrecognizable to myself. After U.S. striker Folarin Balogun received a red card on Wednesday in a match with Bosnia and Herzegovina, I very quickly slipped into the conspiratorial online discourse about the referee, Raphael Claus, who issued it to him. Monday’s matchup (5 p.m. Pacific) between the U.S. and Belgium in Seattle will give many of us another opportunity to lose our collective minds. (Fox will broadcast the game; a free trial of YouTube TV will get you through the rest of the tournament.) There will, of course, be the excitement that happens on the pitch. But as a Seattle resident, I will also happily partake in the combination of national and local pride that comes from showing the world that Americans, too, can provide a top-notch atmosphere for an international soccer event. Here’s to a happy Sixth of July!—Nick Wingfield

Watching: “The Twilight Zone” 

When Rod Serling, creator, writer and host of “The Twilight Zone,” described his show’s netherworld setting as the mysterious fifth dimension, he was, of course, speaking metaphorically. His stories took place in an eerie reflection of an unsettled America, and six decades after the anthology series concluded its five-season, 156-episode run, the anxieties, obsessions and foibles that Serling saw beneath our country’s surface are very much the same ones that underpin our lives today. Take “The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street,” which underscored America’s unease with outsiders—or I could say immigrants. (“Will the Real Martian Please Stand Up?” and “The Invaders” did the same.) “The Masks” looks at the ugliness of wealth and status and will make you see the value in generation-skipping trusts. “Time Enough at Last” is a cry to log off from work before it’s too late, and the underlying warning of “Beauty Is in the Eye of the Beholder” resonates just as powerfully in the looksmaxxing era as it did in the time of careful lipstick and beehive hairdos. Certainly, “The Twilight Zone” has seeped deep into broader pop culture to have long ago reached the point of much-parodied original, but Serling’s ability to conjure fabulist timelessness has lost none of its initial potency.

The show is available in its entirety on Paramount+, and the Syfy Channel does an annual multiday marathon around July Fourth: The most classic episodes, like the ones I mentioned above, air in the evenings, but I particularly enjoy the lesser-seen ones Syfy puts on during the day. These are such installments as “The Howling Man,” which dwells on the unending inevitability of armed conflict; “The Hunt,” a heartwarmer for dog lovers; and “A World of His Own,” a tidy little narrative about a jovial writer who’d totally run amok in a world of AI slop.—A.B.

Watching: “Toy Story 5”

Pixar’s “Toy Story” franchise remains a commercial juggernaut, having accumulated more than $1.6 billion in ticket sales alone since 1995. Except for the most recent movie, “Toy Story 5,” I’ve seen each of the films with my kids—who, yes, aren’t really kids anymore—so I get why it has proven to be one of the more durable properties in Hollywood. Evoking warm memories of a specific kind of suburban American childhood can be a lucrative endeavor. The first “Toy Story” (still my favorite) was essentially an animated rivals-to-buddies movie, and the rest have mainly stuck to the same formula. The cowboy, Sheriff Woody (voiced by Tom Hanks), always ready to ride to the rescue, and the astronaut, Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), unafraid of exploring uncharted terrain, represent two classic American male archetypes and heroes. Their ability to put aside their differences and work together toward the common good is one of our essential national myths, a story we like to tell ourselves as much as our children. 

In “Toy Story 5,” Buzz, with his shiny plastic shell, has more or less withstood the ravages of time. Woody is a little worse for the wear, sporting a paunch and a bald spot. The other adults in the theater laughed when Woody showed up, perhaps in recognition of their own aging physiques. 

Every good film franchise understands the importance of introducing compelling new villains, and “Toy Story 5” suggests, at least at first, that our new common enemy is tech. There is a montage of glassy-eyed children indoors zoned out on screens, and they cyberbully Bonnie (child actress Scarlett Spears), a little girl who still wants to play with toys. Or at least she does until her parents give in and buy Bonnie a frog-shaped smart tablet named Lilypad (Greta Lee). Bonnie soon has eyes only for Lily. With Woody and Buzz in tow, Bonnie’s once-favorite toy, Jessie the Cowgirl (Joan Cusack), leads the charge to help Bonnie make an IRL friend who loves toys too. Lily is devious and uses her superior tech intelligence to outmaneuver the old toys. Of course, Jessie, Woody and Buzz eventually prevail—with the help of old pals like Slinky Dog (Blake Clark) and Rex (Wallace Shawn), a neurotic dinosaur toy—and a happy ending ensues. 

As much as I liked the movie, a key message left me skeptical. At one point, Lily repents over the harm she has caused Bonnie and puts herself in a donation box to be given away. Lily’s absence doesn’t last long, though. For one thing, it turns out that cowgirl Jessie cannot connect Bonnie with a promising new friend without embracing tech. When Lily eventually returns, Woody silences the other toys’ criticism of Lily’s actions by telling them, “She’s one of us, guys—deal with it.” The idea that there’s no further debate to be had over how tech is changing childhood strikes me as one of the biggest American myths of them all.—Amy Dockser Marcus

items.originalTitle: Midjourney wants Hollywood studios to reveal the details of their AI usage
items.summary:
Midjourney, an AI startup, is seeking a court order to require three Hollywood studios—Disney, Universal, and Warner Bros.—to disclose their internal use of AI amid ongoing copyright infringement lawsuits. The studios have accused Midjourney of generating images of copyrighted characters without authorization, while Midjourney argues its use falls under fair use. The dispute now centers on the scope of discovery, with Midjourney requesting broader access to the studios' AI usage documents beyond consumer-facing content to support its defense.

Midjourney contends that the studios may be using AI internally for purposes like storyboarding or content ideation, which could demonstrate industry norms around training AI on copyrighted material. The startup also wants the studios to provide all prompts and outputs related to Midjourney, not just those linked to alleged infringement. The studios' legal team has dismissed these requests as a fishing expedition, emphasizing their goal is to prevent unauthorized copying of their intellectual property rather than to halt AI development or Midjourney's business.

items.originalTitle: Pickleball Is the Past. The Tech Elite Is Obsessed With Padel
items.summary:
In 2023, Matias Gandulfo and Lucas Tepman launched Bay Padel, the first club in San Francisco dedicated to padel, a racket sport blending tennis and squash that is popular in Argentina and Mexico. Despite initial skepticism from landlords, they established their first venue in a former airplane hangar on Treasure Island. Since then, Bay Padel has expanded to locations in San Francisco's Dogpatch neighborhood and Sunnyvale, becoming a popular social and networking hub for tech executives and companies such as OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Amazon, which frequently host employee events there.

Bay Padel now hosts around 30 events monthly and has become intertwined with the competitive AI talent market, with the founders noting that two of their club managers were recently recruited by AI companies as chiefs of staff. The clubs have thus become more than just sports venues, serving as key gathering spots amid the tech industry's ongoing talent competition.

items.originalSummary:
Back in 2023, Matias Gandulfo and Lucas Tepman set out to build the first club in San Francisco devoted to padel, a racket sport that combines elements of tennis and squash. It originated in Mexico and is popular in their native Argentina, attracting millions of players. But potential California landlords for the club thought they were nuts: No way would padel take off in America, too. The two eventually found a space to conduct their experiment: a former airplane hangar on Treasure Island.

“Nobody believed in the idea, of course,” said Gandulfo.

As it turns out, Gandulfo and Tepman were entirely correct about padel’s appeal. Today their Bay Padel now has clubs in San Francisco’s Dogpatch neighborhood and in Sunnyvale, with those venues turning into networking and socializing hot spots for founders, VCs and tech executives. Companies like OpenAI, Meta Platforms, Google and Amazon regularly rent out courts for employee events, and Bay Padel hosts about 30 different events a month. It has even gotten caught up in the AI talent wars. “We recently lost our two club managers to AI companies that hired them as chiefs of staff,” said Tepman.

items.originalTitle: What is Mistral AI? Everything to know about the OpenAI competitor
items.summary:
Mistral AI, a French AI startup founded in 2023, has raised $3.5 billion at a $23 billion valuation as it aims to make advanced AI accessible beyond centralized control by states or corporations. The company plans to release an open-weight language model this summer and is expanding its AI cloud infrastructure in Europe, including significant investments in data centers in France and Sweden.

Mistral's approach focuses on deploying AI models and platforms tailored to enterprise customers, helping them build custom models with their own data. Despite not yet having the leading language models, Mistral has rapidly increased its annual recurring revenue and continues to invest heavily in research and infrastructure to compete with major AI labs. The company also acquired infrastructure startup Koyeb to support its vision of providing secure and affordable AI technology as a commodity for organizations.

items.originalTitle: Open-source tool pxpipe hides text in PNGs to cut Claude Code and Fable 5 token costs up to 70%
items.summary:
The open-source tool pxpipe reduces token costs for AI models like Claude Code and Fable 5 by converting long text prompts into compact PNG images. This method leverages Anthropic's pricing model, which charges for images based on pixel size rather than text length, resulting in cost savings of up to 70% by compressing extensive text content into images.

Pxpipe acts as a local proxy that renders static parts of prompts, such as system instructions and documentation, as images while passing recent messages as text. Although this approach significantly lowers costs, it introduces trade-offs in accuracy and processing speed, as some exact strings may be misread and image processing is slower than direct text input. The tool supports Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5.6, with benchmarks showing varying accuracy across models.

items.summary:
The fanfiction community has recently introduced a tool designed to detect texts generated by the AI model Claude on the Archive of Our Own (AO3) platform. This tool identifies specific coding artifacts left by Claude when text is copied directly from the AI into AO3, marking such works with a red background to signal AI involvement. The initiative reflects ongoing concerns within fan communities about the use of generative AI in creative writing and aims to preserve the human element in fanfiction.

However, the detection method has limitations and has sparked debate over its accuracy and fairness. It only detects unedited text pasted directly from Claude, missing works edited through other software, and cannot determine the extent of AI use in a given piece. Some community members have used the tool to publicly call out authors, raising concerns about potential false positives and the broader implications for fanfiction culture. The tool's creator and others emphasize the importance of maintaining trust and creativity in fandom spaces amid the growing presence of AI-generated content.

items.summary:
Anthropic developer Thariq Shihipar highlights that with Claude's latest model, Fable 5, the main limitation to output quality is the user's own blind spots rather than the AI itself. He emphasizes the importance of users identifying their unknowns—gaps in knowledge they may not be aware of—before crafting prompts to improve the AI's performance.

Shihipar suggests techniques such as blindspot passes, structured interviews, and brainstorming sessions to systematically uncover these knowledge gaps. He advises balancing prompt specificity to avoid overly rigid or too vague instructions, and recommends using Claude to explore unknowns by providing context about the user's current understanding and experience. Additionally, he advocates for documenting decisions during implementation and creating summary reports to enhance clarity and learning throughout the development process.

items.originalTitle: Cloudflare Details Unified Data Platform Where Billing Workloads Account for 53% of Queries
items.summary:
Cloudflare has introduced Town Lake, an internal unified data platform designed to consolidate access to operational, billing, security, and business data across various systems. Alongside Town Lake, the company developed Skipper, an AI-powered analytics agent that enables natural language queries, simplifying data analysis and reporting. Billing workloads constitute 53% of the platform's usage, with 91,760 billing-related queries processed by 324 employees during the reported period.

The platform employs a lakehouse architecture integrating technologies such as Apache Trino, Apache Iceberg, Cloudflare R2 object storage, and DataHub for metadata management. Town Lake supports governed cross-system analytics without moving data between systems, while Skipper translates user requests into validated queries using metadata and schema information. Cloudflare emphasizes a closed governance model with automated and human review processes to ensure data security and compliance.

Looking forward, Cloudflare plans to deepen Skipper's integration with internal workflows and expand the platform's capabilities by migrating additional workloads to R2 SQL. The unified platform and AI agent aim to streamline complex data tasks, improving efficiency in billing analysis, customer support, business intelligence, and security operations.

items.title: Oracle halves Always Free Ampere A1 compute limits from 4 OCPUs and 24 GB RAM to 2 OCPUs and 12 GB RAM without public announcement, causing user confusion over PAYG account impact
items.originalTitle: Oracle Quietly Halves Free Tier Ampere A1 Compute Limits with No Public Announcement
items.summary:
Oracle has reduced the Always Free Ampere A1 compute limits on its cloud platform from 4 OCPUs and 24 GB RAM to 2 OCPUs and 12 GB RAM without any public announcement. This change, effective June 15, 2026, was only reflected in updated documentation, leading to confusion among users, especially regarding the impact on Pay-As-You-Go (PAYG) accounts. While documentation states the new limits apply to all tenancies, support agents have given conflicting information, with some indicating the limits affect only free-tier accounts.

The reduction halves the previously generous free tier allowance, which attracted many developers and hobbyists. Users discovered the change when instances were shut down or when they noticed the updated limits online. Concerns arose that PAYG users might incur unexpected charges if their usage exceeded the new limits, though some support responses suggest PAYG accounts may retain the original limits. However, Oracle has not issued an official clarification, and the documentation remains ambiguous, causing uncertainty about the policy's exact scope and future enforcement.

I’m joking, of course, but it almost feels like some people must be putting AI chip servers in their gardens, given the rush of people wanting to start a neocloud business. (That’s the tech world’s term for firms that rent AI servers to others.)

SoftBank on Thursday announced the creation of a U.S. neocloud venture, joining hundreds of other firms now crowding the sector. Funding still appears to be plentiful: A bunch of the younger neoclouds have raised venture funding in recent days, most recently Together AI’s $800 million fundraising unveiled on Wednesday. Meanwhile, Nvidia, which makes the dominant AI chip, is promising to financially backstop younger cloud firms in exchange for a share of their revenues, we reported on Wednesday night. Nvidia’s move raises the question of why neoclouds need a backstop if demand for computing capacity is so intense.
